H1.text: A race track tilts at its curves. So does a flyover ramp, and a cycling track.

H2.text: A leaning road looks unsafe. So why build one?

H3.text: Aarav rides up the flyover near college. On the curve, the road tilts, with its outer edge higher.

H4.text: Why tilt it at all? And how much tilt is just right?

H5.text: By the end of this video, you will find the right angle with one short formula.

P2.text: A banked road is a curve with its outer edge raised. It tilts toward the centre by an angle theta.

P3.text: In episode sixty eight, a flat curve needed friction to push the car in.

P4.text: On a banked road, the road's normal force leans inward, so part of it points to the centre.

P5.text: So the road itself can turn the car, even with no friction.

S1.text: A one tonne car on a fifty metre curve, seen from behind.

S2.text: On a flat road, theta is zero. The normal force points straight up. It cannot turn the car.

S3.text: Now tilt the road. The normal force tilts too, by the same angle theta.

S4.text: Its sideways part, N sine theta, points to the centre. That is the centripetal force.

S5.text: More tilt, more inward push, so a faster ideal speed. The dot climbs the graph.

S7.text: At the ideal speed, thirteen point four metres per second, friction is zero.

S8.text: Go faster, and the car tends to slide up and out. Friction acts down the slope.

S9.text: Go slower, and it tends to slide down and in. Friction acts up the slope.

D1.text: Now the formula, step by step. No friction first.

D2.text: Step one. Up and down. The upward part of N, N cos theta, balances the weight, m g.

D3.text: Step two. Sideways. N sine theta gives the centripetal force, m v squared over r.

D4.text: Step three. Divide the two. Tan theta equals v squared over r g. So the ideal speed is root r g tan theta.

D5.text: Step four. Now add friction down the slope, at its limit, mu N.

D6.text: Step five. Solve them. The top speed is root of r g, times mu plus tan theta, over one minus mu tan theta.

T1.text: Remember this. On a banked road, the normal force leans in and helps turn the car.

C2.text: A flat road: only friction turns the car. Top speed, root mu r g.

C3.text: A banked road: the normal force helps. Put theta to zero in the big formula, and you get the flat road back.

C4.text: Now you try. A curve is banked for thirteen metres per second. On ice, with no grip, a car goes round at exactly thirteen. Does it make the turn? Pause and decide.

C5.text: Yes! At the ideal speed, N sine theta alone gives the centripetal force. No friction is needed.

K1.text: One more. A car goes slower than the ideal speed. Which way does friction act on it? Pause and think.

K2.text: Up the slope! A slow car tends to slide down the tilt, so friction holds it up.

R1.text: So why tilt the flyover? Follow the links.

R2.text: One. Turning needs an inward force, m v squared over r.

R3.text: Two. On a tilted road, the normal force leans inward.

R4.text: Three. Its sideways part does some, or all, of the turning.

R5.text: Four. So the tyres need less friction. Less wear, and safer when wet.

W2.text: A flyover curve of radius forty metres is built for ten metres per second. Find the bank angle, then the top speed with mu zero point three.

W3.text: Tan theta is v squared over r g. One hundred, over forty times nine point eight. About zero point two five five.

W4.text: So theta is about fourteen point three degrees.

W5.text: Top speed. Root of r g, times mu plus tan theta, over one minus mu tan theta.

W6.text: That is root of three ninety two, times zero point six zero one. About fifteen point four metres per second.

X2.text: Many students write N equals m g cos theta, as for a block resting on a slope.

X3.text: But at the ideal speed, N cos theta equals m g. So N is m g over cos theta, bigger than the weight.

E1.text: Where is this asked? In bank angle and top speed numericals.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A curve of radius ninety metres is banked for fifteen metres per second, and g is ten. A car takes it at exactly fifteen. Find the normal force divided by the car's weight. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is A. Root seventeen over four.

A2.text: Tan theta is v squared over r g. Two twenty five over nine hundred, one quarter.

A3.text: With no friction, N equals m g over cos theta. So N over m g is one over cos theta.

A4.text: That is root of one plus tan squared. Root seventeen over sixteen. Root seventeen over four, about one point zero three.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Which force turns a car on a banked road with no friction?

Y3.text: Two. Why is the normal force on a banked curve bigger than the car's weight?

Y4.text: Three. A car goes faster than the ideal speed. Which way does friction act?
